Veracity means the quality of being truthful or accurate. It describes truthfulness — either as a character trait in a person, or as a property of information, claims, or statements.

Think of it as "truth-ness." When someone or something has veracity, it has the quality of being true.
Two ways the word is used

1. When describing a person

When you say a person has veracity, you mean they are habitually truthful — it's not about telling the truth once, but about being the kind of person who can be consistently trusted to be honest. It's a character quality.

"The judge trusted the witness because of her known veracity."

(She has a solid reputation for always telling the truth.)

"He built his entire career on veracity and integrity."

(Honesty and truthfulness are the foundation of who he is.)

2. When describing a claim, report, or piece of information

When you question or confirm the veracity of something — a news story, a scientific finding, a historical document, a testimony — you are asking: Does this actually match reality? Is this factually correct?

"Scientists spent years testing the veracity of those results."

(They checked whether the results were genuinely accurate.)

"The veracity of the document was confirmed by three independent experts."

(The document turned out to be factually legitimate and accurate.)
How veracity differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Veracity vs. Honesty — Honesty is broader. An honest person doesn't cheat, doesn't steal, doesn't deceive in many different ways. Veracity is a specific slice of honesty — it refers purely to truth-telling and factual accuracy.

Veracity vs. Sincerity — Sincerity means you genuinely believe what you're saying. But you can be sincere and still be wrong — you believed something false and said it. Veracity goes further: it means what you're saying is actually true, not just well-intentioned. A flat-earther can be sincere but lacks veracity.

Veracity vs. Accuracy — Accuracy is about correctness and precision, often used for data, measurements, or technical information. It carries no moral weight. Veracity, on the other hand, can carry a moral dimension — especially when used about a person — because it implies a conscious commitment to the truth.

Veracity vs. Truthfulness — These are the closest synonyms and mean almost exactly the same thing. The only real difference is that veracity is the more formal, elevated word. In everyday conversation, people say "truthfulness" or "honesty." In law, journalism, academia, or formal writing, they say "veracity."
The register: when and where this word appears

Veracity is a formal word. You won't typically hear it in casual conversation. Instead, it belongs to:

  • Legal contexts — questioning a witness's veracity in court
  • Journalism — verifying the veracity of a source's claims
  • Academic writing — assessing the veracity of research findings
  • Formal speech — praising someone's veracity as a character virtue

In everyday talk, people simply say "I trust her" or "I'm not sure that's true." In formal contexts, they say "I trust her veracity" or "I question the veracity of that claim."

These are the phrases you'll encounter most often:

  • "Question the veracity of..." — to doubt whether something is true or someone is being honest
  • "Challenge someone's veracity" — to argue that a person is not being truthful
  • "Verify the veracity of..." — to check and confirm whether something is accurate
  • "Known for their veracity" — having a reputation for being reliably truthful
  • "Impeccable veracity" — perfectly reliable truthfulness, never in doubt
  • "Questionable veracity" — doubtful truthfulness; something seems off
A full range of example sentences

Reading a word in many different contexts is one of the best ways to truly internalize it.

  1. "No one ever doubted her veracity — she told the truth even when it cost her."
  2. "The journalist's veracity was called into question after errors were found in the report."
  3. "The court must determine the veracity of the witness's account before reaching a verdict."
  4. "Historians spent decades confirming the veracity of these ancient records."
  5. "He is a man of unimpeachable veracity — in thirty years, he has never been caught in a lie."
  6. "The veracity of the government's official statement is being investigated by independent analysts."
  7. "She spoke with such confidence and calm that no one thought to question her veracity."
  8. "The veracity of the photograph was confirmed using forensic analysis."

Veracity is the formal word for truthfulness — it describes either a person's reliable habit of telling the truth, or the factual correctness of a piece of information. If something or someone has veracity, it can be trusted to be true.
